market.content_text: Nov 16, 2026 — Investigative Reporters & Editors (IRE) is pleased to announce that the organization has received a grant from Press Forward Chicago to support a new iteration of the Total Newsroom Training program based in Chicago, Illinois. The $76,934 grant from Press Forward Chicago is part of more than $2.8 million in funding for 18 news organizations, journalism support organizations, and universities in the city. “Newsrooms in Chicago are setting the standard for how journalism can and should be done,” said Jonathan Kealing, IRE’s executive director. “We’re excited to bring IRE’s investigative reporting training and a new model for newsroom support to Chicago to help accelerate the good work being done in those newsrooms. We’re grateful to Press Forward Chicago for investing in the craft of investigative reporting.” More details on how to apply to this program will be available soon. This grant follows IRE’s Total Newsroom Training program, which has trained more than 100 newsrooms across the country over the course of a decade. IRE is a grassroots nonprofit organization that seeks to improve the quality of investigative reporting. The organization began in 1975 after a small group of reporters from around the country gathered to share tips about reporting and writing. Today, it provides members access to thousands of reporting tipsheets and other materials through its Resource Center and hosts conferences and specialized training across the country.

market.content_text: IRE Voices: Cassandra Jaramillo reflects on 10 years of reporting and IRE’s impact "I never thought I would be here, technically, as a reporter. I just found my way in journalism, fell in love with it, and couldn't get enough of it," says Cassandra Jaramillo, Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist and longtime IRE member. "I didn't know when I was in college that I wanted to be an investigative reporter, but I had the instincts of an investigative reporter." Jaramillo got her bachelor's degree in journalism at the University of Texas at Austin. She has reported from her home state since 2016, when she joined The Dallas Morning News. In 2021, she worked for The Center of Investigative Reporting, and in 2022 joined ProPublica as an investigative reporter. Since then, she has illuminated the harsh realities of maternal healthcare and Texas's abortion bans. Jaramillo and her team have drawn, and continue to draw, attention to the real cases that are too often treated as hypotheticals. In 2025, Jaramillo and her team won the Pulitzer Prize in Public Service for their investigation, " Life of the Mother ". In the series, Jaramillo — as well as Kavitha Surana, Lizzie Presser and Stacy Kranitz — tells the stories of pregnant women who died after medical delays due to restrictive laws enacted after Roe V. Wade was overturned. In March 2025, partly in response to Jaramillo and her team's reporting, Republican lawmakers in Texas proposed amending the abortion ban to clarify that doctors can terminate pregnancies for serious medical risks—before the mother's life is threatened. This followed a public letter, signed by 111 Texas doctors, urging a change to the ban. Members of the House of Representatives' Committee on Oversight and Accountability also "demanded" a briefing from Texas's health department explaining how and why its maternal mortality review committee failed to examine two years of deaths, including cases Jaramillo's team reported. Her work is impactful, and heavy. "I've always thought about the work as almost running a marathon," Jaramillo says. "...[Sometimes] I'm thinking, 'I don't know if I'm going to pull off the story'—or, 'I'm now so deep into it, it's going to need to, like, happen,' right? Like there's no choice for failure, almost." She has honed her skills through experience, and mentorship with IRE. As an Ida B. Wells Society Fellow from 2018-19, Jaramillo attended IRE's annual conference. There she met her first mentor, Trish Callahan, at the IRE Mentorship Breakfast (sponsored by the Society that year). "[Mentorship] has been such an important motivation to, like, stick with this," says Jaramillo, "and to think 'Okay, my mentor sees something in me that I don't necessarily see, but you know, while I can still do this work, I'm going to keep doing it.'" From her current position in nonprofit news, she's watched layoffs sweep local news in nearly every state. […]

market.content_text: Over the next two years, NPR will address a longstanding listener plea: improving its app. During a November 12 board of directors meeting, NPR CEO Katherine Maher said the organization will rebuild its digital offerings to be a “service-first, app-first destination” as part of NPR’s 2027-2029 strategic plan, Current reported on Thursday. One goal of the plan is to reach “five million weekly active users on its platforms by 2029” and “to build a monthly engaged digital audience of 40 million.” According to Current, Maher said that the NPR network — which includes more than 200 member radio stations — currently reaches 39 million weekly listeners across broadcast and digital, but the “total potential addressable audience, weekly consumers of news, information and culture who are open to our work, is roughly 153 million Americans. That is nearly four times our current reach.” In Apple’s App Store, NPR’s app has a 4.7-star rating and more than 78,000 reviews, of which the majority are positive. But reviewers have quibbles. [img] [/img] [img] [/img] [img] [/img] [img] [/img] Bryan Moffett , NPR’s senior vice president of transformation, said NPR+ , the broadcaster’s subscription program, brought in $8 million in the 2026 fiscal year, up from $5.5 million in 2025. (NPR+ is available with a donation of $8 a month or more, and offers perks like podcasts without ads.) Maher said new investment in the app will help reach younger audiences and shift NPR’s “median audience age from 60-plus toward 40-plus.” “We love radio, but we have been so wildly successful there that we’ve largely exhausted its further financial growth,” Maher told the board. “And as it shrinks, we must invert our revenue engine to ensure sustainability across all of our platforms, including radio, but to build a wider funnel through digital offerings, third-party platforms, and new investments in marketing and communication that will tell our story and share our value with the world.” Overhauling the app is just one part of NPR’s strategy to keep up with users’ changing consumption preferences. In September, Sarah Scire reported on the broadcaster leaning into video podcasts with the acquisition of Kevin Roose and Casey Newton’s technology podcast Machine Gods . NPR chief operating officer Ryan Merkley told Current in June that NPR was already working on redesigning the app to better serve member stations and their listeners. “Fix the app,” departing public editor Kelly McBride told NPR leaders during the meeting. “It’s not a great experience for the audience and it’s key to moving forward, but you guys seem like you’re on it. So I won’t dwell on that.” Nieman Lab requested a copy of the approved strategic plan but did not receive it by publication time. Read the full story in Current here .

market.content_text: We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop . For July , August, and September , traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data. A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com . Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com , Mlive.com , and NJ.com , among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025. Still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a new website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia . The parent company is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney said. In Florida, Cape Coral Breeze , a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “ Best of Cape Coral ” contest , where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website users to our news coverage,” Eckenrode said, and had some success with that strategy. In September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in New York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump. On the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. […]
